claim: Twenty-four healthy human volunteers participated in the experiment (age ranges from 19 to 28; 17 females and 7 males, all right-handed).
source: Twenty-four healthy human volunteers participated in the experiment (age ranges from 19 to 28; 17 females and 7 males, all right-handed).
evidence: Direct statement about participant demographics in the Methods section.

claim: Sample size was set as a multiple of 6 for counterbalancing, and was set a-priori to n=24 based on previous publications from our lab that had similar designs and focused on similar EEG and eye-tracking outcome variables.
source: Sample size was set as a multiple of 6 for counterbalancing, and was set a-priori to n=24 based on previous publications from our lab that had similar designs and focused on similar EEG and eye-tracking outcome variables (e.g. de Vries et al., 2023; Draschkow et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022; van Ede et al., 2021; van Ede et al., 2020; van Ede et al., 2019a).
evidence: Statement about methodological decision supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Two participants were excluded from the eye-tracking dataset due to the poor quality of their eye-tracking data caused by wearing glasses.
source: Two participants were excluded from the eye-tracking dataset due to the poor quality of their eye-tracking data caused by wearing glasses
evidence: Direct statement about data exclusion criteria.

claim: One participant was excluded from the EEG dataset due to large number of artifacts in their EEG signal.
source: one participant was excluded from the EEG dataset due to large number of artifacts in their EEG signal.
evidence: Direct statement about data exclusion criteria.

claim: Reproduction errors were comparable across the four block types (F(3,69) = 1.378, p=0.257, η2=0.057).
source: We found comparable accuracy (reproduction errors) across the four block types (F(3,69) = 1.378, p=0.257, η2=0.057)
evidence: Statistical test result reported with specific values.

claim: There was a significant main effect of block type on reaction times (F(3,69) = 8.994, p<0.001, η2=0.281).
source: while for RTs we found a significant main effect of block type (F(3,69) = 8.994, p<0.001, η2=0.281).
evidence: Statistical test result reported with specific values.

claim: There was a significant linear trend in reaction times with faster responses in blocks with more reliable cues (F(1,23) = 15.304, p=0.001, η2=0.400).
source: This was corroborated by a significant linear trend (F(1,23) = 15.304, p=0.001, η2=0.400), with faster responses in blocks with more reliable cues.
evidence: Statistical test result showing a linear relationship.

claim: In 80% reliable-cue blocks, reproduction accuracy was higher for validly cued vs. invalidly cued memory items (t(23) = 5.357, p<0.001).
source: This confirmed clear behavioral consequences of cue-induced expectations on memory-guided behavioral performance, with higher reproduction accuracy (lower errors) and faster response speed (lower RTs) when the memory test probed the expected (validly cued) vs. the unexpected (invalidly cued) memory item (80% reliable-cue blocks, accuracy: t(23) = 5.357, p<0.001
evidence: Statistical comparison between valid and invalid cue trials.

claim: In 80% reliable-cue blocks, response times were faster for validly cued vs. invalidly cued memory items (t(23) = –5.651, p<0.001).
source: This confirmed clear behavioral consequences of cue-induced expectations on memory-guided behavioral performance, with higher reproduction accuracy (lower errors) and faster response speed (lower RTs) when the memory test probed the expected (validly cued) vs. the unexpected (invalidly cued) memory item (80% reliable-cue blocks, accuracy: t(23) = 5.357, p<0.001, RT: t(23) = –5.651, p<0.001
evidence: Statistical comparison between valid and invalid cue trials.

claim: In 60% reliable-cue blocks, reproduction accuracy was higher for validly cued vs. invalidly cued memory items (t(23) = 3.850, p=0.012).
source: 60% reliable-cue blocks, accuracy: t(23) = 3.850, p=0.012
evidence: Statistical comparison between valid and invalid cue trials.

claim: In 60% reliable-cue blocks, response times were faster for validly cued vs. invalidly cued memory items (t(23) = –5.286, p<0.001).
source: 60% reliable-cue blocks, accuracy: t(23) = 3.850, p=0.012, RT: t(23) = –5.286, p<0.001
evidence: Statistical comparison between valid and invalid cue trials.

claim: The cue-validity effect on reaction time was significantly larger following 80% vs 60% reliable cues (t(23) = –3.497, p=0.002).
source: For RT, this was corroborated by a significantly larger cue-validity effect following 80% vs 60% reliable cues (t(23) = –3.497, p=0.002)
evidence: Statistical comparison of cue-validity effects between conditions.

claim: The cue-validity effect on accuracy did not significantly differ between 80% and 60% reliable cues (t(23) = –1.533, p=0.139).
source: though for accuracy this difference did not reach significance (t(23) = –1.533, p=0.139).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing no significant difference.

claim: Clear alpha lateralization was found in each of the four cue-reliability conditions (cluster p: 100% imperative: p<0.001; 100%: p<0.001; 80%: p<0.001; 60%: p=0.004).
source: In each of our four cue-reliability conditions, we found a clear alpha lateralization (cluster p: 100% imperative: p<0.001; 100%: p<0.001; 80%: p<0.001; 60%: p=0.004)
evidence: Statistical test results for alpha lateralization across conditions.

claim: Alpha lateralization showed a characteristic posterior topography.
source: In each of our four cue-reliability conditions, we found a clear alpha lateralization (cluster p: 100% imperative: p<0.001; 100%: p<0.001; 80%: p<0.001; 60%: p=0.004), with a characteristic posterior topography (Figure 2a).
evidence: Statement supported by reference to figure showing topographic distribution.

claim: Spatial alpha lateralization was graded as a function of cue reliability, being most pronounced for more reliable cues.
source: Consistent with prior work (Fu et al., 2022; Gould et al., 2011; Günseli et al., 2019; Haegens et al., 2012), the spatial alpha lateralization was graded as function of cue reliability, being most pronounced for more reliable cues (Figure 2b).
evidence: Statement supported by citations and figure reference.

claim: There was a significant main effect of cue reliability on alpha lateralization (F(3,66) = 4.711, p=0.005, η2=0.176).
source: A repeated measures ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of cue reliability (F(3,66) = 4.711, p=0.005, η2=0.176)
evidence: Statistical test result for main effect.

claim: There was a significant linear trend in alpha lateralization with stronger lateralization following more reliable cues (F(1,22) = 10.725, p=0.003, η2=0.328).
source: and a significant linear trend (F(1,22) = 10.725, p=0.003, η2=0.328), with stronger alpha lateralization following more reliable cues.
evidence: Statistical test result showing linear relationship.

claim: Spatial saccade bias was observed following the cue in the imperative 100% condition (cluster p=0.002).
source: Similar to our EEG-alpha marker, this saccadic marker of internal attention shifts was also most pronounced when the cue was 100% reliable, though qualitatively similar effects were observed following 80% and 60% reliable cues Figure 2c, d; cluster p: 100% imperative: p=0.002
evidence: Statistical test result for saccade bias.

claim: Spatial saccade bias was observed following the cue in the 100% condition (cluster p=0.002).
source: cluster p: 100% imperative: p=0.002; 100%: p=0.002
evidence: Statistical test result for saccade bias.

claim: Spatial saccade bias was observed following the cue in the 80% condition (cluster p=0.002).
evidence: Statistical test result for saccade bias.

claim: Spatial saccade bias following the cue in the 60% condition was not statistically significant (cluster p=0.341).
evidence: Statistical test result showing non-significance.

claim: The difference between toward and away saccades was predominantly driven by saccades in the micro-saccade range (<2° visual degree).
source: The difference between toward and away saccades (with red colors denoting more toward saccades) was predominantly driven by saccades in the micro-saccade range (<2° visual degree) rather than looking back to the original location of the items that were centered at 6 degrees during encoding.
evidence: Statement supported by saccade-size-over-time plots in Figure 2c.

claim: There was a significant main effect of cue reliability on saccade bias (F(3,63) = 11.049, p<0.001, η2=0.345).
source: The saccade bias was also graded as a function of cue reliability, as confirmed by a significant main effect of cue reliability (F(3,63) = 11.049, p<0.001, η2=0.345)
evidence: Statistical test result for main effect.

claim: There was a significant linear trend in saccade bias with a more pronounced spatial saccade bias when the cue was more reliable (F(1,21) = 18.695, p<0.001, η2=0.471).
source: and a significant linear trend (F(1,21) = 18.695, p<0.001, η2=0.471), with a more pronounced spatial saccade bias when the cue was more reliable.
evidence: Statistical test result showing linear relationship.

claim: Only the 80% cue-reliability condition showed alpha lateralization according to the location of the tested memory item that was larger following unexpected/invalid vs. expected/valid memory tests (cluster p=0.048).
source: For alpha lateralization, we found only weak spatial modulation in response to the test stimulus, with only the 80% cue-reliability condition showing a lateralization according to the location of the tested memory item that was larger following unexpected/invalid vs. expected/valid memory tests (Figure 3a, cluster p=0.048
evidence: Statistical test result with figure reference.

claim: A significant saccade bias in the direction opposite from the memorized location of the tested item was observed in the imperative-100% condition (cluster p=0.021).
source: When the test was certain (100%), a significant saccade bias in the direction opposite from the memorized location of the tested item was observed (Figure 3b, cluster p=0.021, p=0.003, for imperative-100% and 100% conditions, respectively).
evidence: Statistical test result with figure reference.

claim: A significant saccade bias in the direction opposite from the memorized location of the tested item was observed in the 100% condition (cluster p=0.003).
source: When the test was certain (100%), a significant saccade bias in the direction opposite from the memorized location of the tested item was observed (Figure 3b, cluster p=0.021, p=0.003, for imperative-100% and 100% conditions, respectively).
evidence: Statistical test result with figure reference.

claim: In the 80%-valid block, a pronounced saccade bias towards the memorized location of the tested item was found (cluster p=0.023 for valid-cue trials, p<0.001 for invalid-cue trials).
source: In contrast, and of key interest here, when the nature of the test stimulus was not 100% certain (in 80/60% cue-reliability conditions), we found a pronounced saccade bias towards the memorized location of the tested item (Figure 3b, 80%-valid block: cluster p=0.023, p<0.001
evidence: Statistical test results with figure reference.

claim: In the 60%-valid block, a pronounced saccade bias towards the memorized location of the tested item was found (cluster p=0.009 for valid-cue trials, p<0.001 for invalid-cue trials).
source: 60%-valid block: cluster p=0.009, p<0.001, for valid-cue and invalid-cue trials, respectively).
evidence: Statistical test results.

claim: There was no statistical difference in onset latency of saccade bias following expected and unexpected memory tests in the 80% condition (t(21) = –0.567, p=0.577, BF01=3.877).
source: For onset latency after the memory test, we found no statistical difference following expected and unexpected memory tests (80%: t(21) = –0.567, p=0.577, BF01=3.877 in favor of the null hypothesis
evidence: Statistical test result with Bayesian factor supporting null hypothesis.

claim: There was no statistical difference in onset latency of saccade bias following expected and unexpected memory tests in the 60% condition (t(21) = –0.440, p=0.665, BF01=4.108).
source: 60%: t(21) = –0.440, p=0.665, BF01=4.108 in favor of the null hypothesis).
evidence: Statistical test result with Bayesian factor supporting null hypothesis.

claim: There was a clear difference in the offset latency of re-orienting bias in gaze in the 80% condition (t(21) = 2.200, p=0.039).
source: In contrast, we found a clear difference in the offset latency of this re-orienting bias in gaze (80%: t(21) = 2.200, p=0.039
evidence: Statistical test result showing significant difference.

claim: There was a clear difference in the offset latency of re-orienting bias in gaze in the 60% condition (t(21) = 3.409, p=0.003).
evidence: Statistical test result showing significant difference.

claim: There was no evidence for a significant difference in the cue-validity effect on prolonged re-orienting following memory tests between the 80% and 60% cue-reliability blocks (t(21) = 0.237, p=0.815, BF01=5.962).
source: For completeness, we also directly compared the valid-vs-invalid difference in offset latency between the 80% and 60% conditions. We found no evidence for a significant difference in the cue-validity effect on this prolonged re-orienting following memory tests in the 80% and 60% cue-reliability blocks (t(21) = 0.237, p=0.815, BF01=5.962 in favor of the null hypothesis).
evidence: Statistical test result with Bayesian factor supporting null hypothesis.

claim: Fractional area latency analysis revealed a significantly prolonged saccade bias following unexpected tests vs. expected tests in the 80% condition (411 ms vs. 463 ms, t(14) = 2.358, p=0.034).
source: Consistent with our jackknife-based latency analysis, the FAL analysis revealed a significantly prolonged saccade bias following the unexpected tests (the invalid-cue trials) vs. expected tests (the valid-cue trials) in both 80% and 60% cue-reliability conditions (411 ms vs. 463 ms, t(14) = 2.358, p=0.034
evidence: Statistical test result from FAL analysis.

claim: Fractional area latency analysis revealed a significantly prolonged saccade bias following unexpected tests vs. expected tests in the 60% condition (417 ms vs. 468 ms, t(15) = 2.168, p=0.047).
source: 417 ms vs. 468 ms, t(15) = 2.168, p=0.047; for 80% and 60% condition, respectively).
evidence: Statistical test result from FAL analysis.

claim: There was no significant statistical difference in onset latency following unexpected vs. expected tests in the 80% condition (346 ms vs. 374 ms, t(14) = 2.052, p=0.060).
source: Again, there was no significant statistical difference in onset latency following unexpected vs. expected tests. (346 ms vs. 374 ms, t(14) = 2.052, p=0.060
evidence: Statistical test result showing non-significance.

claim: There was no significant statistical difference in onset latency following unexpected vs. expected tests in the 60% condition (353 ms vs. 401 ms, t(15) = 1.577, p=0.136).
source: 353 ms vs. 401 ms, t(15) = 1.577, p=0.136; for 80% and 60% condition, respectively).
evidence: Statistical test result showing non-significance.

claim: Participants used the cue even when the cue was 80% or 60% reliable, and did so in a graded manner that depended on cue reliability.
source: Together, these results show that participants used the cue even when the cue was 80% or 60% reliable, and did so in a graded manner that depended on cue reliability.
evidence: Summary statement based on behavioral performance data.

claim: The brain relies on memorized locations to orient to specific objects held within the spatial layout of working memory.
source: These studies have made clear, among others, how the brain relies on memorized locations to orient to specific objects held within the spatial layout of working memory (de Vries et al., 2023; Draschkow et al., 2022; Fu et al., 2022; Günseli et al., 2019; Kuo et al., 2009; Lepsien et al., 2005; Li et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2022; Macedo-Pascual et al., 2022; Myers et al., 2015; Poch et al., 2017; Poch et al., 2014; Schneider et al., 2015; van Ede, 2018; van Ede et al., 2021; van Ede et al., 2020; van Ede et al., 2019a; van Ede et al., 2019b; Wallis et al., 2015; Wolff et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Studies on external attention have extensively characterized the mechanisms of both orienting of attention following predictive probabilistic cues and re-orienting of attention following unexpected perceptual targets.
source: Studies on external attention have extensively characterized the mechanisms of both orienting of attention following predictive probabilistic cues and re-orienting of attention following unexpected perceptual targets (Carrasco, 2018; Corbetta et al., 2002; Corbetta et al., 2000; Doricchi et al., 2010; Posner, 1980; Posner et al., 1982; Posner and Cohen, 1984).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research on external attention.

claim: Studies on internal attention have almost exclusively focused on the mechanisms supporting initial orienting following predictive retrocues.
source: In contrast, studies on internal attention – directed to representations held in working memory – have almost exclusively focused on just the former: the mechanisms supporting initial orienting following predictive retrocues (for reviews, see Myers et al., 2017; Oberauer, 2019; Sahan et al., 2020; Souza and Oberauer, 2016; van Ede and Nobre, 2023) or temporal expectations (van Ede et al., 2017; Zokaei et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to review articles and primary research.

claim: Lateralization of 8–12 Hz posterior EEG-alpha activity is an established marker of spatial orienting of attention within the spatial layout of visual working memory.
source: Building on ample prior studies, we tracked spatial orienting of attention within the spatial layout of visual working memory using two established markers: the lateralization of 8–12 Hz posterior EEG-alpha activity (Fu et al., 2022; Günseli et al., 2019; Li et al., 2023; Macedo-Pascual et al., 2022; Myers et al., 2015; Poch et al., 2017; Poch et al., 2014; Schneider et al., 2016; Schneider et al., 2015; van Ede, 2018; van Ede et al., 2019a; Wallis et al., 2015; Wolff et al., 2017)
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Spatial biasing of (micro)saccades is an established marker of spatial orienting of attention within the spatial layout of visual working memory.
source: and the spatial biasing of (micro)saccades (as in de Vries et al., 2023; Draschkow et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022; van Ede et al., 2021; van Ede et al., 2020; van Ede et al., 2019a).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Attention enables us to select and prioritize relevant information and can be directed not only to external sensations but also to internal representations held in working memory.
source: Attention enables us to select and prioritize relevant information and can be directed not only to external sensations but also to internal representations held in working memory (Griffin and Nobre, 2003; Panichello and Buschman, 2021; Souza and Oberauer, 2016; van Ede and Nobre, 2023).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Following a probabilistic pre-cue, participants may initially orient their attention to the left where a visual target is expected, but if the target unexpectedly comes on the right, attention requires to be re-oriented to the right.
source: For example, following a probabilistic pre-cue, participants may initially orient their attention to the left where a visual target is expected, but if the target unexpectedly comes on the right, attention requires to be re-oriented to the right (Posner, 1980).
evidence: Example statement supported by citation to classic work.

claim: Retrocues were either 100% reliable, 80% reliable, or 60% reliable, yielding memory tests for items that were certain (100%), expected (80/60% reliable and valid), or unexpected (80/60% reliable but invalid) to be probed for report.
source: Retrocues were either 100% reliable, 80% reliable, or 60% reliable, yielding memory tests for items that were certain (100%), expected (80/60% reliable and valid), or unexpected (80/60% reliable but invalid) to be probed for report.
evidence: Direct description of experimental design.

claim: Following expected tests, internal attentional deployment was not contingent on prior orienting, suggesting an additional verification – 'double checking' – in memory.
source: Following expected tests, internal attentional deployment was not contingent on prior orienting, suggesting an additional verification – 'double checking' – in memory.
evidence: Interpretive statement based on data analysis.

claim: Following unexpected tests, re-focusing of alternative memory content was prolonged.
source: Following unexpected tests, re-focusing of alternative memory content was prolonged.
evidence: Summary statement based on latency analysis.

claim: When the memory test probed the unexpected memory item, attentional re-orienting did not take off later but did become prolonged, consistent with slower responses following unexpected (invalidly cued) memory tests.
source: Moreover, when the memory test prompts selection of the unexpected memory content, we unveil how re-orienting in mind does not take off later, but does last longer, consistent with slower responses following unexpected (invalidly cued) memory tests.
evidence: Summary statement based on latency and behavioral data.

claim: The experimental procedures were reviewed and approved by the Scientific and Ethical Review Board (VCWE) of the Faculty of Behavior & Movement Sciences, VU University Amsterdam (reference number: VCWE-2021–009).
source: The experimental procedures were reviewed and approved by the Scientific and Ethical Review Board (VCWE) of the Faculty of Behavior & Movement Sciences, VU University Amsterdam (reference number: VCWE-2021–009).
evidence: Statement about ethical approval.

claim: All participants provided written informed consent, and consent to publish prior to participation.
source: All participants provided written informed consent, and consent to publish prior to participation
evidence: Statement about informed consent procedures.

claim: Participants were reimbursed 10 euros per hour as compensation for their time.
source: and were reimbursed 10 euros per hour as compensation for their time.
evidence: Statement about participant compensation.

claim: Each participant completed 1000 trials lasting about 2 hours in total.
source: In total, each participant completed 1000 trials lasting about 2 hours in total.
evidence: Statement about experimental duration and trial count.

claim: Memory items were presented at 6° eccentricity to the left and right of central fixation.
source: The memory items were presented at 6° eccentricity to the left and right of central fixation
evidence: Statement about stimulus presentation parameters.

claim: The memory test item was presented in the center of the screen.
source: The memory test item (at the report stage) was presented in the center of the screen
evidence: Statement about test stimulus presentation.

claim: EEG signals were recorded using a 64-channel Biosemi system at 1024 Hz sampling rate.
source: EEG signals were recorded using a 64-channel Biosemi system (1024 Hz sampling rate)
evidence: Statement about EEG recording parameters.

claim: The signal was re-referenced offline to the average of both mastoids.
source: We re-referenced the signal offline to the average of both mastoids.
evidence: Statement about EEG preprocessing.

claim: A fast independent component analysis (ICA) was applied to the EEG epochs to remove components associated with blinks and eye movements.
source: A fast independent component analysis (ICA), as implemented in the Fieldtrip, was then applied to the EEG epochs to remove components associated with blinks and eye movements.
evidence: Statement about artifact removal procedure.

claim: After trial removal, there were on average 241 (sd = 12.0) trials left for informative 100% condition.
source: After trial removal, we had on average 241 (sd = 12.0), 244 (sd = 6.8), 243 (sd = 8.7), 243 (sd = 7.2) trials left for informative 100%, 80%, 60%, and imperative 100% conditions, respectively.
evidence: Statement about trial counts after preprocessing.

claim: A 300 ms sliding time window was used to estimate the spectral power between 2 and 40 Hz.
source: A 300 ms sliding time window was used to estimate the spectral power between 2 and 40 Hz (in steps of 1 Hz) that was advanced over the data in steps of 10 ms.
evidence: Statement about time-frequency analysis parameters.

claim: The eye tracker was positioned ∼5 cm in front of the monitor on a table (~65 cm away from the eyes).
source: The eye tracker (EyeLink 1000, SR Research SR) was positioned ∼5 cm in front of the monitor on a table(~65 cm away from the eyes).
evidence: Statement about eye-tracking setup.

claim: Horizontal and vertical gaze position was continuously recorded for single eye at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz.
source: Horizontal and vertical gaze position was continuously recorded for single eye at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz.
evidence: Statement about eye-tracking recording parameters.

claim: The onset of a saccade was determined as the first sample where the velocity surpassed a trial-based threshold set at five times the median velocity.
source: We then determined the onset of a saccade as the first sample where the velocity surpassed a trial-based threshold set at five times the median velocity.
evidence: Statement about saccade detection algorithm.

claim: A minimum delay of 100 ms between successive saccades was enforced to prevent multiple classifications of the same saccade.
source: To prevent multiple classifications of the same saccade, we enforced a minimum delay of 100 ms between successive saccades.
evidence: Statement about saccade detection criteria.

claim: Saccade magnitude and direction were determined by assessing the disparity between pre-saccade gaze position (from –50–0 ms before threshold crossing) and post-saccade gaze position (from 50 to 100 ms after threshold crossing).
source: Saccade magnitude and direction were determined by assessing the disparity between pre-saccade gaze position (from –50–0 ms before threshold crossing) and post-saccade gaze position (from 50 to 100 ms after threshold crossing).
evidence: Statement about saccade parameter calculation.

claim: Saccade rates were quantified using a sliding time window of 50 ms, progressing in 1 ms increments.
source: Following saccade identification and labeling, we quantified the time courses of saccade rates (in Hz) using a sliding time window of 50 ms, progressing in 1 ms increments.
evidence: Statement about saccade rate calculation method.

claim: The spatial saccade bias was calculated as the differences (in Hz) between toward and away saccades.
source: For our main analyses, we focused directly on the spatial bias in saccades, calculated simply as the differences (in Hz) between toward and away saccades.
evidence: Statement about primary outcome measure calculation.

claim: A cluster-based permutation approach was employed to statistically assess the temporal profiles of the spatial modulations in EEG activity and eye movements.
source: To statistically assess the temporal profiles of the spatial modulations in EEG activity (alpha lateralization) and eye movements (spatial saccade bias), we employed a cluster-based permutation approach (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007) using the fieldtrip 'ft_timelockstatistics' function with 'montecarlo' method.
evidence: Statement about statistical analysis method with citation.

claim: 10,000 permutations were conducted to construct the permutation distribution of the largest cluster.
source: We conducted 10,000 permutations to construct the permutation distribution of the largest cluster that would be obtained by chance
evidence: Statement about statistical analysis parameters.

claim: Attentional deployment after the memory test only occurs when the cue leaves some uncertainty regarding which memory item will be tested.
source: First, we show that attentional deployment after the memory test only occurs when the cue leaves some uncertainty regarding which memory item will be tested.
evidence: Summary statement based on comparison across cue-reliability conditions.

claim: When the cue is 100% reliable, participants may drop the other memory item or transform the relevant item into a different format that does not invoke spatial revisiting after the memory test.
source: When the cue is 100% reliable, participants may drop the other memory item (Astle et al., 2012; Gözenman et al., 2014; Gressmann and Janczyk, 2016; Griffin and Nobre, 2003; Gunseli et al., 2015; Oberauer, 2001; Pertzov et al., 2013; van Moorselaar et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2013) or transform the relevant item into a different format (cf. Larocque et al., 2014; LaRocque et al., 2013; Lewis-Peacock et al., 2012; Myers et al., 2017; Rose et al., 2016; Stokes, 2015; Wolff et al., 2017) that does not invoke spatial revisiting after the memory test.
evidence: Interpretive statement supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Participants may transform the relevant item into the appropriate action plan when 100% certain.
source: For example, participants may transform the relevant item into the appropriate action plan, when 100% certain (Henderson et al., 2022; Nasrawi et al., 2023; Nasrawi and van Ede, 2022; Olivers and Roelfsema, 2020; Schneider et al., 2020; van Ede et al., 2019b).
evidence: Interpretive statement supported by citations.

claim: When the other item cannot be dropped, the memory items likely preserve their spatial organization, inviting spatial deployment of attention following the memory test.
source: In contrast, when the other item cannot be dropped, in the case of cues that leave some uncertainty, the memory items likely preserve their spatial organization, inviting spatial deployment of attention following the memory test.
evidence: Interpretive statement based on experimental findings.

claim: Participants engage in a second-stage verification ('double checking') in mind whenever cues do not predict memory tests with certainty.
source: In other words, participants may engage in a second-stage verification ('double checking') in mind, whenever cues do not predict memory tests with certainty.
evidence: Interpretive statement based on data showing attentional deployment after expected tests.

claim: Spatial deployment (re-orienting) of attention in mind was prolonged when the test prompted a report for the memory item that was not expected to become tested.
source: Specifically, spatial deployment (re-orienting) of attention in mind was prolonged when the test prompted a report for the memory item that was not expected to become tested.
evidence: Summary statement based on offset latency analysis.

claim: Unexpected memory tests do not delay the process of re-orienting in mind to the appropriate memory content.
source: Thus, while unexpected memory tests do not delay the process of re-orienting in mind to the appropriate memory content, attentional deployment did become prolonged when re-focusing the unexpected memory item
evidence: Summary statement based on onset and offset latency analyses.

claim: Prolonged attentional deployment following unexpected tests likely reflects prolonged effort to extract the relevant information from the memory item that was not expected to be tested.
source: attentional deployment did become prolonged when re-focusing the unexpected memory item, likely reflecting prolonged effort to extract the relevant information from the memory item that was not expected to be tested.
evidence: Interpretive statement about mechanism.

claim: Only gaze showed a clear pattern of re-orienting in response to the test stimulus, while both EEG-alpha and gaze markers robustly tracked spatial orienting following the retrocue.
source: Though we found both EEG-alpha and gaze markers to robustly track spatial orienting following the retrocue, only gaze showed a clear pattern of re-orienting in response to the test stimulus.
evidence: Summary statement comparing the two markers.

claim: The test stimulus was a large central stimulus that may have attenuated alpha activity, possibly making it challenging to find spatial modulations in alpha activity.
source: In our task, the test stimulus was a large central stimulus that may have attenuated alpha activity, possibly making it challenging to find spatial modulations in alpha activity (see e.g. van Ede et al., 2014), without similarly affecting gaze.
evidence: Interpretive statement with citation to prior work.

claim: Participants revisit tested memory content even when contents were already previously attended, suggesting a second verification ('double checking') in mind.
source: We unveil that participants revisit tested memory content even when contents were already previously attended – suggesting a second verification ('double checking') in mind.
evidence: Summary statement based on trial-sorting analysis.

claim: When tests prompted unexpected memory content, re-orienting in mind became prolonged, putatively reflecting a prolonged effort to re-sample unexpected content from memory.
source: Moreover, when tests prompted unexpected memory content, we found that re-orienting in mind became prolonged, putatively reflecting a prolonged effort to re-sample unexpected content from memory.
evidence: Summary statement with mechanistic interpretation.

claim: These findings bring attentional re-orienting to the domain of working memory.
source: These findings bring attentional re-orienting to the domain of working memory
evidence: Summary statement about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The study reveals a second stage of internal attentional deployment following both expected and unexpected memory tests.
source: Besides internal orienting after predictive cues, we unveil a second stage of internal attentional deployment following both expected and unexpected memory tests.
evidence: Summary statement from the abstract.

claim: Attentional orienting and re-orienting are two separate attentional stages.
source: This underscores a classic distinction between two separate attentional stages: attentional orienting and re-orienting.
evidence: Statement about established theoretical framework.

claim: Whether deployment of spatial attention within visual working memory also occurs in response to ensuing memory tests has remained elusive.
source: Yet, whether deployment of spatial attention within visual working memory also occurs in response to ensuing memory tests – and how this depends on whether working memory tests prompt mnemonic content that is certain, expected, or unexpected to become tested – has remained elusive.
evidence: Statement identifying a gap in the literature.

claim: By presenting memory items laterally, but memory tests centrally, spatial markers can be used to test whether attention re-orients inside the mind when specific memory content becomes tested.
source: By presenting memory items laterally, but memory tests centrally, we could use these spatial markers to test whether attention also re-orients inside the mind when specific memory content becomes tested – and to assess how such re-orienting depends on prior expectations regarding the to-be-tested memory content.
evidence: Statement about the experimental design rationale.

claim: Cue-validity effects on reproduction accuracy were 2.948 degrees better after valid vs. invalid cues in the 80% condition.
source: As can be seen in Figure 1b and c, effects of cue validity were also larger following 80% (2.948 degrees and 219 ms better after valid vs. invalid cues)
evidence: Quantitative statement with figure reference.

claim: Cue-validity effects on reaction time were 219 ms better after valid vs. invalid cues in the 80% condition.
source: effects of cue validity were also larger following 80% (2.948 degrees and 219 ms better after valid vs. invalid cues)
evidence: Quantitative statement with figure reference.

claim: Cue-validity effects on reproduction accuracy were 2.221 degrees better after valid vs. invalid cues in the 60% condition.
source: vs. 60% (2.221 degrees and 100 ms better after valid vs. invalid cues) reliable cues.
evidence: Quantitative statement with figure reference.

claim: Cue-validity effects on reaction time were 100 ms better after valid vs. invalid cues in the 60% condition.
source: vs. 60% (2.221 degrees and 100 ms better after valid vs. invalid cues) reliable cues.
evidence: Quantitative statement with figure reference.

claim: The bias observed during internal attentional focusing was predominantly driven by fixational micro-saccades rather than looking back to the encoded location of the memory items.
source: This further corroborates that the bias observed during internal attentional focusing was predominantly driven by fixational micro-saccades rather than looking back to the encoded location of the memory items (Johansson and Johansson, 2014; Richardson and Spivey, 2000; Spivey and Geng, 2001; Wynn et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by complementary analysis and citations.

claim: The saccade bias was larger following imperative-100% vs. 100% reliable cues.
source: It's worth noting that while alpha lateralization shows very comparable amplitudes in the imperative-100% and 100% conditions, the saccade bias was larger following imperative-100% vs. 100% reliable cues.
evidence: Observation about differential pattern between markers.

claim: The difference between imperative-100% and 100% conditions in saccade bias may reflect a difference that is selectively picked up by the gaze marker or may reflect differential sensitivity of the two markers to different sources of noise.
source: This may reflect a difference between these two cueing conditions that is selectively picked up by our gaze marker (though it may also reflect differential sensitivity of our two markers to different sources of noise).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of observed difference.

claim: A direct comparison between the two markers is non-trivial as they are two distinct dependent variables.
source: While the two markers each had their own characteristic patterns, a direct comparison between the two markers is non-trivial (as they are two distinct dependent variables) and was beyond the scope of the current study
evidence: Statement about methodological limitations.

claim: The saccade bias in the direction opposite from the memorized location of the tested item in 100% conditions likely reflects 'return' saccades to the center in response to the memory test stimulus from lingering gaze-position biases following the cue.
source: This likely reflects 'return' saccades to the center in response to the memory test stimulus from lingering gaze-position biases following the cue (i.e. a residual effect from the cue-induced modulation).
evidence: Interpretive statement about mechanism.

claim: The saccade bias shows re-orienting to the mnemonic contents in mind in response to the memory test.
source: Because the test stimulus was presented in the center, this saccade bias shows re-orienting to the mnemonic contents in mind, in response to the memory test.
evidence: Interpretive statement about what the marker reflects.

claim: Re-orienting in mind was found not only following unexpected tests but also following expected tests.
source: Critically, we found this re-orienting in mind not only following unexpected tests (for which the preceding retrocue initially directed attention to the other, non-tested, memory item during the delay), but also following expected tests.
evidence: Summary statement about key finding.

claim: Just like mnemonic focusing after the cue, re-orienting after the memory test was also predominantly reflected in fixational micro-saccades.
source: Thus, just like mnemonic focusing after the cue, re-orienting after the memory test was also predominantly reflected in fixational micro-saccades, and not looking back at the original location of the memory items that were encoded at 6 degrees away from central fixation.
evidence: Summary statement comparing cue and test effects.

claim: A link between gaze bias and RTs was established only following expected memory tests in the 80% cue-reliability condition (cluster p=0.001).
source: We also sorted patterns of gaze bias after the memory test by performance but could only establish a link between this gaze bias and RTs following expected memory tests in our 80% cue-reliability condition (cluster p=0.001, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Statistical result with figure reference.

claim: The lack of significant statistical differences in the remaining conditions may possibly reflect a lack of sensitivity (insufficient trial numbers) for the additional analysis.
source: The lack of significant statistical differences in the remaining conditions may possibly reflect a lack of sensitivity (insufficient trial numbers) for this additional analysis.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of null results.

claim: Significant clusters were found when comparing the saccade bias following expected and unexpected memory tests in both 80% and 60% cue-reliability blocks (cluster p=0.003, p=0.025).
source: First, we found significant clusters when comparing the saccade bias following expected (validly cued) and unexpected (invalidly cued) memory tests, in both 80% and 60% cue-reliability blocks, as indicated by the black horizontal significance lines in Figure 3b (cluster p=0.003, p=0.025).
evidence: Statistical results with figure reference.

claim: The observed differences between the saccade bias following expected and unexpected memory tests in both 80% and 60% cue-reliability conditions are robust even when carefully matching the number of trials.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3, this complementary sub-sampling analysis confirmed that our observed differences between the saccade bias following expected and unexpected memory tests in both 80% and 60% cue-reliability conditions are robust even when carefully matching the number of trials between validly cued (expected) and invalidly cued (unexpected) memory test.
evidence: Statement about robustness check with figure reference.

claim: Clear gaze signatures of attentional deployment were found in response to expected memory tests, whether or not trials had shown such deployment after the cue in gaze.
source: As we show in Figure 4a and b, we found clear gaze signatures of attentional deployment in response to expected (valid) memory tests, no matter whether we had pre-selected trials in which we had also seen such deployment after the cue in gaze (cluster ps: 0.115, 0.041, 0.027,<0.001 for 80%-valid, 60%-valid, 80%-invalid, 60%-invalid trials, respectively), or not (cluster ps: 0.016, 0.009, 0.001,<0.001 for 80%-valid, 60%-valid, 80%-invalid, 60%-invalid trials, respectively).
evidence: Statistical results from trial-sorting analysis with figure reference.

claim: A more pronounced gaze bias to the memorized location of the tested item was found in the invalidly cued trials in the 60% cue-reliability condition when comparing trials with and without toward-saccade after cue (cluster p=0.032).
source: We only found one difference between the trials sorted by their response to the cue: with a more pronounced gaze bias to the memorized location of the tested item in the invalidly cued trials in the 60% cue-reliability condition (Figure 4d: cluster p=0.032).
evidence: Statistical result with figure reference.

claim: The more pronounced gaze bias in invalidly cued trials when having relied on the cue may reflect the prolonged need to re-orient to the other memory item.
source: This may reflect the prolonged need to re-orient to the other memory item, when previously having relied more on the cue to prioritize the memory item that did not end up being tested in these invalidly cued trials.
evidence: Interpretive statement about mechanism.

claim: There was no evidence that the test-locked bias was contingent on the prior use of the cue (ts=–0.226,–0.047, −1.717,–0.399, ps=0.824, 0.963, 0.101, 0.694, BF01=3.930, 5.856, 1.613, 5.673).
source: Again, we found no evidence that the test-locked bias was contingent on the prior use of the cue (bar graphs Figure 4a–d: ts=–0.226,–0.047, −1.717,–0.399, ps=0.824, 0.963, 0.101, 0.694, BF01=3.930, 5.856, 1.613, 5.673 in favor of the null hypothesis across all four conditions).
evidence: Statistical results with Bayesian factors supporting null hypothesis.

claim: Observers deploy attention to the memorized location in response to the memory test, whether or not they had already oriented their attention after the cue.
source: These results suggest that observers deploy attention to the memorized location in response to the memory test, whether or not they had already oriented their attention after the cue.
evidence: Summary statement based on trial-sorting analysis.

claim: Deployment of attention after the memory test may reflect an additional verification stage following expected memory tests and a genuine re-orienting of attention to the other memory item following unexpected memory tests.
source: In other words, this suggests that deployment of attention after the memory test may reflect an additional verification stage following expected memory tests (in valid-cue trials), and a genuine re-orienting of attention to the other memory item following unexpected memory tests (in invalid-cue trials).
evidence: Interpretive statement about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Several prior studies have demonstrated how attention can dynamically orient and re-orient to previously encoded memory items in anticipation of the memory test.
source: To date, several prior studies have demonstrated how attention can dynamically orient and re-orient to previously encoded memory items in anticipation of the memory test, such as following sequential retrocues (de Vries et al., 2020; de Vries et al., 2018; Rose et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2020), or following expectations that designated one item relevant early and another late (van Ede et al., 2017; Zokaei et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement about prior research with citations.

claim: The findings of attentional re-orienting specifically concern spatial re-orienting in response to the memory test, not in anticipation of this test.
source: In contrast, our findings of attentional re-orienting specifically concern spatial re-orienting in response to the memory test; not in anticipation of this test.
evidence: Statement distinguishing current findings from prior work.

claim: Ample prior studies have considered processes related to retrieval at the memory test or reselection at memory encoding.
source: While ample prior studies have considered processes related to retrieval at the memory test (Ester and Pytel, 2023; Nobre et al., 2007; Schneider et al., 2015; Souza et al., 2016), or reselection at memory encoding (Chen et al., 2019; Chen and Wyble, 2015; Fu et al., 2023)
evidence: Statement about prior research with citations.

claim: The study uniquely focused on deployment of spatial attention to the tested memory item, not general, non-spatial cognitive processes related to retrieval.
source: we uniquely focused on deployment of spatial attention to the tested memory item (not general, non-spatial cognitive processes related to retrieval, or attentional reselection to decide what features to be encoded into working memory).
evidence: Statement distinguishing current focus from prior work.

claim: The study was in a unique position to isolate spatial deployment of attention following the test because the memory test was always centrally presented while memory items were presented lateralized.
source: We were in a unique position to isolate such spatial deployment of attention following the test, because our memory test was always centrally presented while our memory items were presented lateralized.
evidence: Statement about methodological advantage.

claim: It is notoriously hard to know whether attentional allocation was graded at the single-trial level.
source: While we observe clearly graded modulations in the trial average, it is notoriously hard to know whether attentional allocation was also graded at the single-trial level (Stokes et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about methodological limitation with citation.

claim: Following 80% reliable cues, it could be that participants consistently deployed 80% of their full 'attention potential', or deployed their full attention potential in 80% of the trials.
source: For example, following 80% reliable cues, it could be that participants consistently deployed 80% of their full 'attention potential', or deployed their full attention potential in 80% of the trials.
evidence: Statement about alternative interpretations of graded effects.

claim: This is the first demonstration of a graded modulation of the gaze marker of attention shifts within the spatial layout of visual working memory.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a graded modulation of this gaze marker of attention shifts within the spatial layout of visual working memory.
evidence: Statement about novelty of finding.

claim: Prior studies from the lab have only shown the gaze marker following retrocues that were 100% reliable.
source: To date, however, we have only ever shown this following retrocues that were 100% reliable.
evidence: Statement about prior work from the same lab.
